2.2 — Spikes: Physics, Damage & Death

You built a coin you can walk through. Now build a spike you cannot. That sounds like a small change — one checkbox — and it is going to break your game, because it will reveal something you have been carrying since 1.4: your character is a ghost. Today you fix that properly, and then build health, damage and death on top of the fix.

The Problem: Walk Into a Spike ~10 min

Step 1. The Overworld scene has no spikes placed at all. Drag two or three Assets/Prefabs/Spikes instances into the scene and put them somewhere you will walk.

Step 2. Open the Spikes prefab and give it a collider, the same way you gave the coin one in 2.1. This one is not a trigger — spikes are solid, so leave Is Trigger unchecked. Its tag is already Spikes.

Step 3. Press Play and walk into your spike.

Tinker: The Ghost

  1. You gave the spike a solid collider. Walk into it. Did you stop, or pass straight through? Describe exactly what happened.
  2. Now walk into a wall. You gave the Player a Collider2D and a Rigidbody2D in 2.1 — so why does the wall still not stop you?
  3. Open the documentation for Transform.Translate. Find the sentence that says whether the physics engine is consulted, and quote it precisely.
  4. The spike, the wall and the coin all have colliders now. What single thing in the Player's movement code stands between your character and the physics world?
  5. Predict: if you keep transform.Translate and make the spike solid, what will your player be able to do to every wall in the game?
This is the most important bug in the unit — do not patch around it. Your character is a ghost that the physics engine knows about but is never asked to move. transform.Translate edits coordinates directly; it never consults physics, so it will happily place you inside a wall. Every collision feature from here to the end of the year — spikes, walls, doors, enemies, the boss — depends on the decision you are about to make in the next block. Make it deliberately, and be ready to defend it.
Read the Docs: Choose Your Movement Method ~20 min

You read this table in 1.5 as a prediction. Now it is a decision you have to live with for the rest of the year, so read the last two columns very carefully:

TechniqueHow it worksStops at walls?What it requires
transform.Translate(vector) Offsets coordinates directly. Never consults physics. No Nothing. This is what you have now.
Rigidbody2D.MovePosition(position) Sweeps the body to a target position, testing the path as it goes. Yes A Rigidbody2D, usually Body Type Kinematic. Ignores forces.
Rigidbody2D.linearVelocity = vector Assigns velocity; the physics engine performs the motion. Yes A Rigidbody2D, Body Type Dynamic. Carries momentum.
Rigidbody2D.AddForce(vector) Applies a physical push, factoring in mass, drag and inertia. Yes A Dynamic Rigidbody2D with a mass you will have to tune.

Choose, Then Justify

  1. Your character is a ghost. Which row fixes that with the smallest change to the code you have already written?
  2. This game is about exploring a world and being shot at by turrets. Do you want your movement to carry momentum? Which row gives you momentum whether you want it or not?
  3. The "what it requires" column is the real decision. Which cost can you live with all year, and which one would you regret in Unit 6 when you add jumping?
  4. Rows 2, 3 and 4 all need Rigidbody2D settings beyond the default. Name the settings you must change — and what goes wrong if you forget each one. (You already changed one of them in 2.1.)
  5. MovePosition wants a Kinematic body, and a Kinematic body ignores forces. If you choose it, how will a turret ever knock your player backwards?
  6. Your EnemyController, TurretController and Projectile are all still empty shells. Would an enemy or a bullet need a different row from the player? Argue a position.
  7. What evidence from your own build would make your justification convincing to another student — a measurement, a screenshot, a before-and-after?
Build Lab: Make the Switch and Prove It ~20 min

Rewrite the movement inside PlayerController.Update() to use the method you chose, and set the Rigidbody2D up to match. Then prove it:

  • Walk into a wall — do you stop?
  • Walk into a spike — do you stop?
  • Set your speed absurdly high and run at a thin wall — do you pass through it?
Kinematic and Dynamic are not interchangeable. MovePosition expects a Kinematic body. Assigning linearVelocity on a Kinematic body does nothing at all — silently, with no error. If your character ignores your input completely after this change, check Body Type before you check anything else.
One API gotcha you will meet in every tutorial you read. This project runs Unity 6, where the Rigidbody2D velocity property is called linearVelocity. Almost every tutorial, forum answer and video you will find online was written for Unity 5 or 2022 and calls it velocity instead. If a snippet you find does not compile, check the Unity version it was written for before you assume you typed it wrong — reading the date on a source is part of reading the source.

Justify Your Choice — this is your written decision record

  1. Which movement method did you choose? Name the exact API call you now use.
  2. What did you have to change in the Rigidbody2D Inspector to make it work, and what broke when you got one of those settings wrong?
  3. What evidence from your build proves the choice works? Say what you ran into, and what happened.
  4. Name one thing your chosen method makes harder, which you are accepting for now. Every choice costs something — a choice with no stated cost is not yet a decision.
Read the Docs: How Should a Spike Hurt You? ~15 min

A spike is solid, so it stops you. But "stopping you" and "hurting you" are two separate decisions. Here are the three honest ways to build a hazard:

ApproachWhat the player feelsWhat firesThe risk
Solid spike + OnCollisionEnter2D You stop against it. Damage once per touch. OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D collision) You can get wedged against the spike, and sliding along it may not register at all.
Trigger spike + OnTriggerEnter2D You walk through it. Damage once per entry. OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other) Standing inside the spike deals no further damage — usually wrong for a hazard.
Trigger spike + OnTriggerStay2D with a cooldown Repeated damage while you stand in it. OnTriggerStay2D(Collider2D other) It fires every frame. Without a cooldown you lose all your health instantly.
The parameter types are different, and it matters. OnTrigger* hands you a Collider2D, which has .gameObject and .CompareTag directly. OnCollision* hands you a Collision2D, which is a data container carrying contact points, relativeVelocity, and .gameObject. That is why one lets you write other.CompareTag(...) and the other makes you write collision.gameObject.CompareTag(...).

Picking a Hazard Model

  1. Which of the three matches the game you are building? Which would you pick for a game where spikes are a puzzle to be solved rather than a hazard to be avoided?
  2. In the third row, what happens on the very first frame the player stands in the spike if you forget the cooldown? How many times per second does OnTriggerStay2D run?
  3. For which of the three can you write other.CompareTag("Spikes") directly, and what must you write for the others?
  4. Should a spike be destroyed when it damages you, the way a coin is destroyed when collected? What kind of object is a spike, and what does that tell you about using Destroy here?
Build Lab: Health, Damage & Death ~20 min
Architectural specification: health.
  • Following the decision you made in 2.1, where does health live, and what field holds it? What type, what starting value, and how is it exposed as a tuning knob?
  • What method changes health by a signed amount? Why one method taking a positive or negative argument, rather than separate Heal and Damage methods? (Think about who will call it later.)
  • Which callback holds the spike check, and how do you identify the spike from inside it?
  • After subtracting health, what do you print so a player can watch the number change with no UI at all?
  • What condition means "the player is dead", and what should happen at that exact moment?
Death has more than one defensible design. Choose one, and defend it.
  • (a) Reload the current scene — SceneManager.LoadScene(SceneManager.GetActiveScene().buildIndex). Everything resets, including the coin count.
  • (b) Reload a scene by name — before you pick this, read Build Settings and answer two questions: which scene is index 0, and does that scene contain a Player?
  • (c) Do not reload at all — reset health and move the player back to a starting position, keeping the coins.

The Death Decision

  1. Which death design did you choose, and what does the player keep and lose under it?
  2. Option (b) loads this project's scene 0. What is in that scene, and what would the player actually see after dying? Test it before you answer.
  3. If you chose (a), what happens to the coin count — and is "you lose your coins when you die" a fair rule, or just an accident of where the number happens to live?
  4. If you added a coin penalty using coins / 2, what does a player with exactly 1 coin lose? Is that fair? Read the docs for Mathf.FloorToInt.
  5. Whatever resets when you die, write down exactly what survives. You will need this fact in Unit 5.

Save and press Play. Walk into a spike. Your player should stop against it, and the Console should report your health dropping. Hit it until health reaches zero and watch what your death design actually does.

Bug Hunt ~15 min

Bug Hunt: Physics and Boundary Faults

  1. Set the spike's collider back to Is Trigger but keep your collision callback. Does anything fire? What does the Console show — or fail to show?
  2. Delete the if (health <= 0) check and stand in a spike. What does the health number do? What does that prove about the difference between a rule and a value?
  3. If you used the OnTriggerStay2D model, remove the cooldown and describe the first half-second of contact.
  4. Set your speed very high and run at a wall. Do you stop, or end up on the other side? What does the wall's thickness have to do with it? (This failure has a name — look up "tunnelling".)
  5. Die on purpose and watch the Console. Which values reset, and which survived? Compare that against what you wrote down earlier — were you right?
  6. Set Body Type to Kinematic and try to move with linearVelocity. What happens, and why is a silent no-op the hardest kind of bug?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Exploring Collision Data

  1. If you used collisions, add Debug.Log("Impact: " + collision.relativeVelocity); and bump a spike from two different angles. What does a Collision2D know that a Collider2D cannot tell you?
  2. Using relativeVelocity.magnitude, how would you make damage happen only above a speed threshold? What would you name that number, and what is the feature usually called in games?
  3. Which movement method would you now recommend for the enemy in Unit 4? Does your answer have to match the player's? Why or why not?
  4. Move your spike onto a slope or a corner and walk into it repeatedly. Does the damage fire once, or several times? What does that tell you about your choice of callback?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain why transform.Translate ignores colliders, and quote the documentation saying so
  • Compare the four movement methods and name what each one requires in the Rigidbody2D
  • Defend your chosen movement method in writing, with evidence from your build
  • Compare the three ways a spike can hurt the player, and say which you chose
  • Explain OnCollisionEnter2D versus OnTriggerEnter2D versus OnTriggerStay2D by their parameter types
  • State exactly what resets and what survives when your player dies
  • Commit and push
